title: Hoshana Rabbah
hookLine: the seventh day: seven circuits, and willows beaten on the ground
tomorrow: Shemini Atzeret: stay one more day

cards: Early morning in a synagogue, the seventh day of Sukkot. On the other mornings of the festival, people have walked once around the reading table holding the palm branch and citrus, chanting.
Today they go around seven times. The line is slow, and somebody's lulav keeps poking the person in front. Then people pick up small bundles of willow twigs and strike them on the floor.
Leaves fly. Kids love this part. Adults, if they're honest, do too.
The day has a name that sounds like a shout.

teach.b: Hoshana Rabbah means the great hoshana. Hoshana is a plea: save, please. It comes from the psalm sung on festivals, in the old Jewish translation: "We beseech Thee, O LORD, save now!"
All week, after each circuit, people chant short prayers called hoshanot, asking for rescue, for rain, for the harvest.
On the seventh day the circuits and pleas pile up to seven, and the day earns the word great. Then the willows.
The Mishnah, in tractate Sukkah, describes willow branches set up around the altar in the Temple, and the people circling it. After the Temple fell, the willow stayed.
The Talmud calls beating the willow a custom of the prophets: not a commandment from the Torah, but very old and kept with care. Why willows?
A midrash notices that the willow has no taste and no smell, and has it stand for people with neither learning nor good deeds.
And the willow grows by water, so it fits a festival where people begin to ask for winter rain. A later layer came from the mystics.
In the Zohar's tradition, Hoshana Rabbah is the very end of the season of judgment that began on Rosh Hashanah, when the sealed verdict is finally sent out.
So some people stay up the night before reading Deuteronomy and Psalms, and greet each other with a wish for a good note.
Striking the willows, in that reading, knocks something loose: the last of the year's heaviness, shaken off and left on the floor.

how: On Hoshana Rabbah, many synagogues make seven circuits with the lulav and etrog while chanting the hoshanot, then each person strikes a small bundle of willow branches on the ground; some communities also keep a night of study beforehand.

games.q: the seven circuits are done and someone hands you a small bundle of willow twigs. what do you do with it?
games.why: the willows are struck on the floor, leaves flying: a custom the Talmud traces to the prophets.

practice: Name one thing you've carried since the fall began, a worry, a grudge, a mistake you keep replaying, and hold it in mind like a bundle of twigs.
If you like, tap your hands on your knees five times, letting each tap loosen it a little. Then rest your hands open and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Hoshana Rabbah. The great save-us. Seven circuits, a bundle of willows, and the year's last judgment let go. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew and Aramaic: the great hoshana, the great save-us.

carryVoice: Your line: beat the willows. What's shaken loose can stay on the floor. Day six hundred sixty-two.
